a4d2ab775d7245fd: SEREMBAN: There is currently no pressure on Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to dissolve Parliament to pave the way for the 16th general election (GE16), says Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) vice-president Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad.

He said the prime minister had his own considerations on the appropriate time to dissolve Parliament, adding that the Federal Government's current term had yet to expire and Anwar continued to enjoy majority support among members of parliament.
"I think we should wait. There is no pressure to make any sudden move to dissolve Parliament.

"We should wait until the end of the term, unless something drastic happens. We should prioritise the positive economic momentum that the people are enjoying today," he told reporters after officiating the 2026 National Wanita Muda Amanah Convention (Warda) at Klana Resort here today.

Dzulkefly, who is also health minister, was commenting on calls for Parliament to be dissolved following the Melaka election, in which BN and PN secured a combined 24 seats while Pakatan Harapan (PH) won four.

He said the people should first be given the opportunity to enjoy the benefits of the Unity Government's efforts, citing positive economic indicators, foreign investments and rising household incomes.

He also said Malaysia's economic performance had received recognition from international analytical bodies, claiming the country ranked among the world's 15 best-performing economies after climbing 19 places.
Dzulkefly said any move that could undermine political and economic stability or national harmony was undesirable, adding that the people's well-being should remain the priority.
fbc113d498111319: ALOR SETAR, Nov 15 — The Kedah state government today tabled its RM1.34 billion Budget 2027, projecting an operating deficit of RM90 million or 10.59 per cent, for the year.

Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Muhammad Sanusi Md Nor said the state government had estimated revenue of RM850 million under the budget, themed ‘The Greater Kedah: Mensejahterakan Rakyat’, while operating expenditure was projected at RM940 million.

He said the revenue target represented an increase of RM12 million from the RM838 million targeted in 2026, with land revenue contributing the largest share at RM551 million, followed by miscellaneous revenue (RM253 million), forestry revenue (RM30 million) and district revenue (RM16 million).
“Of the total operating expenditure allocation, RM81.66 million is set aside for charged expenditure, while RM858.34 million is allocated for supply and services expenditure.

“The 2027 Budget also includes allocations for the State Development Fund, Forest Development Fund and Water Supply Development Fund, with total development expenditure amounting to RM401.28 million,” he said when tabling the Kedah Budget 2027 at the Kedah State Legislative Assembly sitting at Wisma Darul Aman here today.
He said RM245 million of the development allocation was set aside for the State Development Fund, involving 10 implementing departments, while RM12.53 million was allocated for forestry development.

The Water Supply Development Fund received RM143.75 million, comprising RM138.75 million from federal government loans for the implementation of three loan-funded projects and RM5 million from the state government’s allocation.
“The state government also aims to gradually reduce its operating deficit to 10.59 per cent in 2027, from 12.65 per cent in 2025 and 11.81 per cent in 2026.

“This reflects the state government’s commitment to strengthening its fiscal position through expenditure controls, improved management efficiency and optimisation of state revenue sources to ensure long-term financial sustainability,” he said.

The 2027 Budget is the second year of the implementation of the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP), continuing the state’s development agenda based on the Kedah Development Plan 2035 and The Greater Kedah 2050, with emphasis on ensuring that economic progress also improves the people’s well-being. — Bernama
69b1902d1393d77e: AMMAN: Jordan's State Security Court sentenced three men to death on Sunday for carrying out an attack on a church in the southern governorate of Karak last month that killed nine people, the state news agency Petra reported.

The court convicted the men of offences including carrying out terrorist acts resulting in death, possessing weapons and ammunition for terrorist purposes and promoting the ideology of a terrorist group. The ruling is subject to appeal and automatic review by the Court of Cassation, Petra said.
Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud on October 23, in a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority. Authorities said 34 people were also wounded.

Security forces arrested the three men on October 26 after a shootout at an abandoned house in Karak. All three were wounded, while no security personnel were injured, according to the Public Security Directorate.

Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, later that day launched airstrikeson southern Syria against groups it linked to the church attack. Syrian authorities said seven people, including three children and a woman, were killed.
Jordan later acknowledged that its airstrikes had killed civilians in Syria and the two countries agreed to form a joint security committee to review the incident and its consequences. — REUTERS

7d7c559b6f269e54: ADDIS ABABA, Nov 15 — In a cramped workshop in the heart of Addis Ababa, seamstresses are busy turning out reusable sanitary pads — a vital resource in Ethiopia, where many girls go without because of the cost and taboos.

In Ethiopia, a religiously conservative country of 130 million people where around 40 percent live in poverty, menstruation is still often treated as a subject of shame and disposable sanitary pads are luxury items.
Hanan Ahmed, 41, set up her company, Han’s with Care, in 2021 in the hope of tackling what she calls “menstrual shame and period poverty” — something she experienced firsthand when she was younger.

“I used to be one of those girls who have a very heavy flow. I would end up staining my clothes and the desk I was sitting at. And because of that, I didn’t come to school for like a week or two, making up excuses,” Hanan told AFP.

After a career in fashion and then aviation, she realised that “some of the period-shaming that happened 20 years ago is still going on now” and decided to leave everything behind to start her own business.
Ethiopia imports all its sanitary pads from abroad, making them unaffordable to the poor.
A 2017 study by Johns Hopkins University found that just 28 percent of Ethiopian women reported having everything they need for their periods.
The result is that young girls miss school, women lose crucial income and many are forced into dangerous alternatives.
In rural areas, they use “bits of mattress or dirty socks”, said Hanan, adding that it causes infections.
Her company offers cotton sanitary pads that are washable and reusable for up to two years.
‘Excluded’
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A seamstress works sews a reusable sanitary pad beside the illuminated Han’s with Care sign at the company’s Addis Ababa workshop on October 20, 2026. — AFP pic
In the small workshop in the capital, the dozen workers are tightly focused, the clatter of sewing machines drowning out any conversation.
The company can produce up to 1,000 pads a day.
Rather than distributing them through pharmacies, the firm sells to sponsors such as banks, which then give them out for free across the country.
Tsege Woldu Abate, 30, has worked at the company for five years.
She recalled her first period at age 13: “I didn’t tell my family... I was afraid to speak up.”
Today, she says she is “proud” of her work because “it is very useful for girls”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A seamstress’s hands guide a reusable sanitary pad through a sewing machine at the Han’s with Care workshop in Addis Ababa on October 20, 2026. — AFP pic
On a recent morning at the Nigat Kokeb School in Addis Ababa, sanitary pads were distributed to about a dozen young girls.
Their teacher, Tigist Shewangizaw, welcomed the company’s awareness-raising efforts and donations, so that “no girl misses school”.
While Hanan highlights the progress made in the capital, she said the situation remains largely unchanged in rural areas.
“In some tribes and religious groups, when a young girl begins her period, she is excluded from the household,” Hanan said.
She hopes to secure greater support from the Ethiopian authorities and to see the conversation around menstruation normalised.
“We’re trying to create that freedom to talk about periods,” said Hanan. “We’re raising our voices, so I believe and I hope that in 10 years’ time, there will be a change in our community.” — AFP
33b44f38dd86a583: PETALING JAYA: Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN) have been told to publicly state whether their central leadership knew of, and endorsed, the actions of Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim and 10 former state executive council members during the royal crisis.

In a joint statement, DAP vice-chairman Syahredzan Johan and three other prominent party members said the coalitions' leaders had never openly objected to or rejected the actions of their assemblymen.
They said the central leaderships of Umno, PAS, MCA and Wawasan should also seek forgiveness for their assemblymen’s misconduct.

Their statement follows Ismail’s confirmation that he withdrew a letter sent to the Keeper of the Rulers' Seal concerning the purported removal of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
It is believed that the letter also affirmed the 10 sacked exco members' unanimous support for Tuanku Muhriz.

“In effect, they have admitted they were wrong to conspire to remove Tuanku Muhriz as the Yang Dipertuan Besar and replace him with another individual,” said Syahredzan and the three other key DAP members.

“All those involved should publicly seek forgiveness from Tuanku Muhriz and the other Malay rulers for these excessive and disloyal actions, which clearly went beyond the powers permitted under the Negeri Sembilan constitution.

“BN and PN’s central leadership should also publicly state whether they knew of, and endorsed, the actions of the menteri besar and former exco members (as they have) never openly objected to or issued any statement rejecting the actions of their assemblymen in this plot.”

The statement was issued by Syahredzan, DAP national publicity assistant secretary Young Syefura Othman, central executive committee member Sheikh Umar Bagharib Ali and Bukit Bendera MP Syerleena Abdul Rashid.
The four also urged the authorities to disclose the outcome of their investigation into Ismail and the former exco members, saying the actions warranted prosecution.
Negeri Sembilan has been embroiled in a royal crisis since April, when four purported undangs, or chieftains, announced Tuanku Muhriz’s removal as the Yang Dipertuan Besar.
In September, 10 state executive council members, seven of them from Umno, issued a statement purportedly affirming Tuanku Muhriz’s removal. Ismail subsequently endorsed the move.
However, the decision was disputed by the state’s Dewan Keadilan dan Undang and the Attorney-General's Chambers.

Tuanku Muhriz revoked the appointments of all 10 exco members in September. The state administration subsequently gazetted the revocations, stating their appointments had been annulled because they had breached their pledges of allegiance to the ruler.

The 10 include Umno's Mustapha Nagoor (Palong), Faizal Ramli (Linggi), Zaiful Bahri Idris (Chembong), Razi Ali (Sungai Lui), Asna Amin (Lenggeng), Siti Nur Umaira Hasim (Labu) and Suhaimizan Bizar (Gemencheh).
The other three are MCA's Siow Kong Choon (Chennah), PAS's Fairuz Isa (Serting) and Wawasan’s Razali Abu Samah (Sikamat).

d0ceca091ff1c308: SANT'AGATA BOLOGNESE: Lamborghini has abandoned plans to launch fully electric vehicles by 2030, saying it has yet to find technology that would give it an edge over competitors, Sputnik/RIA Novosti reported, quoting the company’s director of marketing and sales, Federico Foschini.
The company had planned to make the successor to its Urus model and the Lanzador crossover coupe fully electric by 2030.
Lamborghini was seeking technical solutions that would give drivers the same emotional experience as its petrol-powered models, known for their distinctive sounds and vibrations.

“We have concluded that, above all, it is not so much about technical characteristics and dynamic capabilities as it is about the emotional component. There are still no technologies that would allow us to stand out from competitors and justify our decision to enter the market of fully electric vehicles,” Foschini said at a closed-door briefing for journalists.
The next-generation models, expected to appear around 2030, will be plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) rather than fully electric vehicles, he added.
China has become the world’s largest producer of electric vehicles.
Chinese automaker BYD is among the world’s leading manufacturers of electric vehicles and batteries.
In Russia, Chinese automaker Changan led EV sales as of the end of October 2026, according to data from analytical company PPK cited by the Autostat agency.
Toyota, Russian brands Evolute and Umo, and BYD completed the top five brands by sales.
36df6bbb1a700f62: AMMAN, Nov 15 — A Jordanian court on Sunday sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out last month’s deadly gun attack on a church in the kingdom’s south.
Gunmen killed nine people and wounded 25 others when they stormed a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan’s Karak governorate on October 23.
Authorities said three men, two Jordanian brothers and their relative by marriage, had fled after the attack and were arrested three days later.

In a statement Sunday, the Jordanian military said the “State Security Court issued its ruling sentencing to death the three criminals who carried out the terrorist attack” at the Greek Orthodox church.

The court found them guilty of “committing terrorist attacks” resulting in death, as well as weapons offences, “conspiracy to commit terrorist acts” and “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation”.
The attack shocked the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians make up around three percent of the population. — AFP

63fe367f3840fbb5: ABIDJAN, Nov 15 — Valerie Bli Lou is a shopkeeper from a modest family, but she is determined to give her late father the sumptuous funeral that Ivorian tradition demands – whether she can afford it or not.

Dancing through the night in a flowing burgundy-and-black tunic at her father’s wake in Yopougon, a working-class neighbourhood in Ivory Coast’s economic capital, Abidjan, the 60-year-old recounted the hardships of organising and paying for this lavish tribute to his life.
Death is big business in Ivory Coast, where families are expected to say goodbye to their loved ones with massive, music-fuelled feasts tinged with moments of both joy and sadness.

Bli Lou said that including the three cows she bought, she had already paid more than 2.5 million CFA francs (US$4,275, RM17,485) for her father’s funeral rites — more than 15 times the average monthly salary in the west African country, according to the World Bank.
There would be more expenses to come, she said: transporting the coffin to a cemetery 500 kilometres (310 miles) away, building a tomb and hosting and feeding hundreds of guests at the burial.
Bli Lou, who is Christian, told AFP she was “proud” to be covering the expense, despite the difficulty.
“My father is like my second God. I must honour him,” she said.
Tears and dancing
When Bli Lou’s father died in July, she did not have the money to organise a funeral in line with tradition.

So, she did what many families do: paid to preserve his body in a morgue, at the rate of about 7,000 CFA francs (RM49) a day, while she got together the funds she needed with the help of family and friends.
She finally managed to put together the wake at a vast centre in Yopougon known for hosting funeral events, where crowds of mourners converge every Saturday.
Families often have to reserve weeks in advance.
The centre was holding four wakes in all on the October night Bli Lou celebrated her father.
Families had hired bands, set up sprawling arrays of tents and decorated chapels with portraits of their late loved ones inside.
The feasts were a mix of tears and music, embraces and dancing.
‘Pressure’
At another wake, a DJ read out the names of those who had contributed cash or otherwise helped with the ceremony.
The family said they had paid more than five million CFA francs (RM34,970) in all, imposing a mandatory contribution on every relative.
Some went into debt to come up with the money.
“There’s a lot of pressure,” said one family member, Mathias Zouh.
“Our parents and grandparents did it, so we do it, too. Otherwise, it would reflect badly on you in the village.”
Funerals are so important in some Ivorian communities they unleash competition and rivalries between families, said anthropologist Leo Montaz, who has studied the subject.
“Everyone wants to show how important he is and reaffirm his social status,” he said.
For Muslims, Ivory Coast’s other major faith, funerals must be organised more quickly — but the multiple ceremonies involved are still often expensive.
The importance of funeral rites has given rise to a booming industry in the country.
In Yopougon, stores offer coffins, funeral clothing, artificial flowers, headstones, jewellery and scents for perfuming the dead.
Gertrude Brou has worked in the industry for 15 years, selling funeral articles and dressing the dead.
“There’s a need for funerals, and it’s a job that earns you a good living,” she said.
Her colleague Georges agreed, saying he had built his house and sent his children to study abroad thanks to his funeral parlour.
“It’s a thriving profession,” he said. — AFP

2b78a264ee7bcfeb: SEREMBAN: The Health Ministry will prioritise efforts to bring Pasir Gudang Hospital in Johor to full operational capacity, from its current level of 85 per cent.

Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said the ministry was implementing an aggressive plan to fill vacant positions to ensure the hospital could operate at full capacity, with 304 beds and 16 delivery rooms.
He said the placement of nurses and medical specialists at the hospital was currently based on its operational capacity.
"Our current operational level is 85 per cent. I have already answered this matter in Parliament. We have not been able to fill all the positions for doctors and specialists.

"However, the current placement of specialists and doctors allows us to operate at 85 per cent. Many departments have already begun operating," he told reporters after officiating the Amanah National Young Women's Convention 2026.
Earlier, the media reported that Johor Menteri Besar Datuk Onn Hafiz Ghazi had raised concerns over the hospital's operational needs.
Of the 2,271 positions allocated to the hospital, only 1,276 had been filled as of Nov 6.
Dzulkefly said the ministry remained committed to meeting Johor's healthcare needs.
Located in Bandar Seri Alam, Pasir Gudang, the hospital began operations in stages on Aug 1, 2025.

Its construction cost RM375.5 million and was aimed at improving access to healthcare for residents of Pasir Gudang and surrounding areas, while helping to ease congestion at Sultanah Aminah Hospital and Sultan Ismail Hospital.

49f738ae84d28b34: GENEVA: The World Health Organization warned on Friday of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.

“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.

Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza's population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the "Yellow Line" – a demarcation established under October’s US-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where, of course, the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Van De Weerdt explained.

The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
"The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip."

COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come," Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.

The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“

COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.
032523ae7f5b8b36: IPOH, Nov 15 — The bursting of a 455-cubic-metre water tank at Taman Kuala Kangsar in Kuala Kangsar yesterday was caused by the condition of its structure, which was more than 40 years old.

Perak Infrastructure, Energy, Water and Public Transport Committee chairman Datuk Seri Mohammad Nizar Jamaluddin said the Kuala Kangsar operations centre of the Perak Water Board (LAP) received information about the incident at about 5pm, which affected water supply to approximately 520 consumers in the surrounding areas.

He said LAP had carried out washing and cleaning works on roads around the burst Taman Kuala Kangsar tank, while direct water supply through the main pipeline to the affected areas, namely Taman Kuala Kangsar and Taman Meranti, had also been implemented.
“The removal of all affected tank panels has been carried out, and plans are being made to replace the tank with a new one.
“In addition, LAP is conducting a comprehensive technical assessment of the old tank structure before installation of the new tank begins,” he said in a statement today.

Mohammad Nizar said preliminary investigations at the scene found that the burst tank had caused water to overflow onto surrounding roads, but no reports of casualties or property damage had been received so far.
“An inspection of the house located nearest to the tank also found that it was safe and had sustained no damage,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mohammad Nizar said water supply in the affected areas remained stable and uninterrupted, and the Kuala Kangsar LAP operations centre would continue to monitor the situation to ensure there were no disruptions to water supply and to prevent a recurrence.
Several videos of the tank bursting incident have gone viral on social media since yesterday, causing panic among residents. — Bernama

bc3e732da7d544fd: MADRID: Almost 1,500 migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands on Saturday, the highest number in a single day since 2020, the EFE news agency reported on Sunday, citing the maritime rescue service.
A total of 1,488 people in 14 boats were rescued by the Spanish coastguard, EFE reported, continuing a surge of arrivals from West African countries to the Spanish archipelago since October.
The previous one-day record was the 1,461 people rescued in waters off the Canary Islands on Nov 7, 2020, maritime rescue services said on Sunday.

While migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with the same period last year, the sharp increase last month placed additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less densely populated ones.
One boat on Saturday was carrying 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children, authorities said. The rescued migrants were taken to El Hierro, one of the smallest Canary Islands.
Most of the people were from Senegal, Gambia and Guinea Conakry.
Twelve boats arrived in El Hierro, plus one in Gran Canaria and another in Tenerife.
Spain's Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres will visit El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the surge in migrant arrivals.
The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings.
Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.
Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings.
Migrant arrivals to the Canary Islands between January and Oct 31 were down 5.5 per cent from the same period last year, government data show.

f4f24ab577634b71: MANILA: The Philippines' foreign minister said on Sunday that Indonesia was very candid in expressing what it had done to address forest fires.

"The leaders also encouraged the Asean member states to prioritise the ratification of the Asean Coordinating Center on Transboundary Haze Pollution Control," Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told a news briefing.

On Friday, a study said thousands of hectares of land on palm oil and pulpwood concessions run by large listed firms were burnt during Indonesia's worst fire season in years, highlighting the role of deforestation and land clearing.

Indonesia's forest fires caused a spike in respiratory illness at home and triggered air pollution warnings and school closures across the region, with fire emissions surging to three times the seasonal average.

A total of 2.88 million hectares of land were damaged by fire from January to October this year, driven by intense El Nino weather conditions and extreme heat, as well as clearing of forests to make way for industrial-scale palm oil and pulpwood plantations, according to a joint study by Rainforest Action Network (RAN) and geomonitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.

Another report quoting scientists said, wildfires that hit large parts of Indonesia from August to October and plunged much of Southeast Asia into hazardous smoke were made much worse by "record-breaking" heat caused by human-induced climate change.

While a very strong El Nino was the dominant factor in determining the extremely low levels of rainfall across Indonesia from July, human-induced climate change contributed around 1.6 degrees Celsius of additional heat during the fire season, said a report by climate research group World Weather Attribution.

"The conditions that we saw this year would simply just not have happened in a world without the human contribution to climate change, even with the very strong El Nino that we're seeing," said Theodore Keeping, a researcher into wildfires and extreme weather at Imperial College London who contributed to the report.
ed1c5c7f644d9076: CUSCO, Nov 15 — Pope Leo XIV will travel high into the Andes to Cusco on Sunday, before plunging into the Amazon basin, testing his post-cancer stamina as he wraps up his South America tour.

The head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, who underwent lung cancer surgery a month ago, refused to cut the visit to the Unesco World Heritage Site from his itinerary, despite Cusco’s location at over 3,400 metres (11,000 feet) of altitude.

Once in the former capital of the Inca Empire, he will climb even further to Saqsaywaman, a massive hilltop fortress overlooking the Peruvian city, where he will meet with representatives of popular Catholic devotion.

The US-born pontiff has been on an intense 12-day trip through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, rallying a declining faith, defending the poor and marginalised, and deploring regional ills, from a rise in violence to a drop in birth rates.

Sunday, Leo’s last full day in Latin America, will be the most demanding physically for the 71-year-old, as he travels between two of the most important cultural and geographic regions in Peru, his adopted homeland.
As Robert Francis Prevost, he served for almost two decades as a missionary in the South American country, and his emotionally-charged homecoming will conclude in a key centre of Catholicism.

Designed by the Incas to resemble in its layout a crouching puma, Cusco was partially destroyed during the Spanish conquest in the 16th century, but would go on to serve as a major base for the evangelisation of the Andes.

The pontiff will spend three hours in Cusco, leading prayer in front of the Cathedral, before flying to Pucallpa, one of the largest cities in the Peruvian Amazon, to meet representatives of Indigenous Amazonian peoples.

Lying on the banks of the Ucayali River deep within the rainforest, the city is home to numerous timber-harvesting businesses and an oil refinery, and serves as a gateway to the surrounding rainforest communities.
An aerial view of Yarinacocha Lagoon in Peru’s Ucayali region on November 14, 2026, ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Pucallpa on November 15. — AFP pic
Leo will watch a dance performed by the Shipibo-Konibo tribe before making a speech expected to focus on threats to Indigenous people, from drug trafficking to illegal deforestation and pollution.
Peru, half of which is covered by the Amazon rainforest, is one of the few countries in the world where uncontacted tribes continue to live in absolute autonomy, away from modern society.

But narcotics gangs look to take advantage of jungle areas that are difficult to access, and the Amazon’s natural riches attract exploiters of its gold or its cedar and mahogany trees, which are in danger of extinction.

To symbolise the importance of preserving the rainforest, Leo will take part in a ceremony to plant a tree – reportedly a shihuahuaco, an Amazonian species that can live for more than 1,000 years but is attractive to loggers.
He will then celebrate a Mass expected to draw tens of thousands of pilgrims, before flying to the capital Lima, where he will depart Monday for Rome.
Despite the slog, Leo has looked fresh-faced every day of the trip.
This final test will be scrutinised, however, as the Church seeks confirmation that the cancer – discovered fewer than 18 months into Leo’s papacy – has been overcome. — AFP

1a21363bb5e2a947: MOSCOW: Ukrainian airstrikes hit the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk on Sunday, local authorities said, with media reporting a fire in one of the country's biggest petrochemical plants.

"Early this morning, Nizhnekamsk was the target of a massive and prolonged attack by enemy drones. As a result of this attack, facilities in the industrial zone were damaged," the city's mayor, Radmir Belyaev, wrote on Telegram.
A residential building was also damaged, he added.
Nizhnekamsk, a city of about 240,000 people, is often dubbed the "petrochemical capital" of Tatarstan. It is home to oil refineries and a major petrochemical plant.
Authorities in the region, quoted by Russian media, said three people were wounded.
Ukrainian and Russian media said the strikes caused a fire at the Nizhnekamskneftekhim (NKNK) petrochemical complex, owned by leading Russian company Sibur.
Videos published on social networks, which AFP has not authenticated, showed flames and thick smoke rising above the industrial site.

An engineer at an electricity substation was killed in separate Ukrainian strikes overnight in Taganrog, an industrial port city in the Rostov-on-Don region, which borders Ukraine, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
Taganrog mayor Svetlana Kambulova said a fire at a substation had been put out and a local state of emergency had been declared.
The defence ministry in Moscow said in a statement that it had shot down 533 Ukrainian drones between Saturday night and Sunday morning over a dozen regions of Russia and annexed Crimea.
There was no immediate response from Kyiv, which says it targets Russian industrial facilities in response to deadly Russian strikes on its own territory.
ba34f92dc86a83c5: LOS ANGELES, Nov 15 — Aryna Sabalenka apologised on Saturday after an on-court outburst during her defeat to Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells.
Footage shared widely on social media appeared to show the former world number one swearing in a tirade that some commenters interpreted as directed towards Svitolina or Ukrainians in general.
However, Sabalenka said Saturday that she lost her cool due to the behaviour of spectators during Friday’s 3-6, 6-3, 1-6 defeat, which sent the four-time Grand Slam-winner crashing out.
“I want to clarify something from my recent match that has been circulating online,” Sabalenka wrote in a post on Instagram.
“My comment was not directed at Elina. I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes and I reacted emotionally in the moment.
“That said, I should have handled my frustration differently and I apologise to anyone I offended. Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament.”

Svitolina, who has refused to shake hands with tennis players from Russia and its regional ally Belarus since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, acknowledged that a match against Sabalenka could carry extra weight for her fans.
“As we see there’s many, many Ukrainians, many, many flags ... and of course they want me to win this particular match,” she said Saturday when asked about Sabalenka’s statement.
“We’ve played many times with Aryna ... she has her fans. I have my fans,” added Svitolina, who reached the Finals title match with a win over Linda Noskova on Saturday.

“I have seen the glimpse of it because obviously it’s in the social media,” she said. “(I) just hope the matches between us (are) respected. Sometimes in some matches that we’ve played also there have been not great comments towards me in regards of the war.
“It is like this in the social media sometimes the things are turned around a little bit.” — AFP

5cdf08726a7e71df: BATU PAHAT: An 11-year-old girl who lost both parents when a tar-laden lorry crushed their multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) in Parit Yaani will undergo plastic surgery for injuries to her left thigh.

d6adab6763cc076a: NEW YORK, Nov 15 — US air travel was expected to return to normal on Sunday after a nationwide ground stop left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo and disrupted travel worldwide.
The Trump administration blamed Friday’s ground stop – meaning no planes can take off – on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford said that 12,000 flights were cancelled on Friday, while tracking website FlightAware showed more than 6,600 cancelled flights on Saturday.
As of Sunday morning, FlightAware had recorded more than 1,200 cancelled flights.
Speaking at a news conference in Washington, Bedford predicted a full resumption of flight schedules by “close of business on Sunday.”
During the outage, footage from airports showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways and passengers thronging concourses, desperate for information.

“Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it’s just a mess, right?” Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, told AFP as she waited for a flight on Saturday morning at New York’s LaGuardia airport.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire to a high-speed fibre cable had caused “issues” with communication with planes and radar feeds.
“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment… it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy told reporters.
In another embarrassment, Saturday’s news conference – where administration officials appealed for more funds to upgrade outdated systems – was delayed due to technical problems with the audio feed.
Returning to normal
Friday’s disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace – which is among the busiest in the world – since the 9/11 attacks.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Departure screens inside Terminal B at New York’s LaGuardia Airport on November 14, 2026, as US flights resume after Friday’s nationwide ground stop. — AFP pic
The nationwide halt was lifted at 8.15pm Eastern Time Friday (0115 GMT Saturday).
FAA officials reopened the airspace “after restoring full functionality” at air traffic control facilities, according to Duffy.

Tim Johnson, consumer director at the UK Civil Aviation Authority, said although US flights have resumed, there could be “some follow-on disruption” as airlines re-book passengers and get all services back to normal.
At LaGuardia airport, some travellers were more sanguine than others about the continued disruption of their flights.
“We’re stuck here for the next, I don’t know, 36 hours,” said Pat Curlett, a 62-year-old Ford worker.
“No one expects the whole airline system to go down,” said 77-year-old traveller Steven Rathe, who was waiting to embark on a four-leg trip from New York to Albuquerque.
“We’re lucky it wasn’t longer. So they’re flying today and for that I’m grateful.”
Ageing infrastructure
The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos – it also raised serious concerns about the country’s ageing infrastructure.

Duffy appealed for US$50 billion (RM204.5 billion) in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to “meet this moment.”
“Cut the crap,” retorted Illinois state governor and prominent Democrat JB Pritzker on X. “Trump and Republicans have controlled Congress and could have funded the system.”
New York Governor Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or be fired by Trump, writing on X: “We’re fortunate no lives were lost.”
US lawmakers called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cyber criminality.
“If today proves anything, it’s that we need to update our air traffic control system & rebuild our airport infrastructure,” Republican Senator Eric Schmitt said on X.

President Donald Trump was uncharacteristically quiet about the outage that had knock-on effects for international flights to and from the United States, making no public statement about the ground stop as of Sunday morning. — AFP
564c5217e8c4468c: PETALING JAYA: Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) MPs will submit a memorandum to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), urging it to investigate the reasons for the termination of the Project Delivery Partner (PDP) model for Phase 1 of the Sabah Pan Borneo Highway project in 2019.
GRS secretary-general Armizan Mohd Ali said the MPs wanted the PAC to examine not only the highway’s current status but also past policy decisions that had affected its progress.

“This is important to ensure that policy changes are not driven by partisan political considerations at the expense of efforts to improve road connectivity for the benefit of Sabahans and the state’s development,” he said in a statement.

Armizan welcomed the PAC’s decision on Oct 19 to investigate the management, financial governance and physical implementation of Phase 1 of the highway project following the release of the Auditor-General's Report Series 2/2026 on Oct 5.

Armizan said the PAC's investigation should be comprehensive and transparent, identifying the causes of the delays and ensuring that all parties involved in decisions concerning the project and its implementation provided explanations.

MyIPO steps up efforts to nurture young innovators

Separately, Armizan, who is also the domestic trade and cost of living minister, said the Malaysian Intellectual Property Corporation (MyIPO) is stepping up efforts to nurture innovation and raise awareness of intellectual property (IP) protection among young people through its IP SPARK 2026 programme.

“One of the key targets under the 13MP is for Malaysia to rank among the world's top 20 countries in the Global Innovation Index by 2030,” he told reporters after closing IP SPARK 2026 today.

Themed "Ideas, Create, and Impact", the two-day programme, which began yesterday at SMK Benoni and SMK Pengalat in Papar, brought together 120 participants comprising school students and trainees from the National Youth Skills Institute.

5e0f19c886174ba6: URGENT pleas for cash from poor nations most exposed to the kind of climate-related disasters that have marked this year risk meeting a sluggish response at Turkiye's COP31 talks as Western governments put national security and living costs first.
Two years ago, rich countries agreed at UN climate talks they would triple climate funding for poorer countries to US$300 billion per year by 2035 versus a previous 2020 target.
Also by 2035, financing from all public and private sources combined would be US$1.3 trillion annually.
The rich countries met their 2020 target two years late.

Since then, climate action has slipped down the political agenda for Western governments as US President Donald Trump has withdrawn international funding, while wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have added to inflationary pressures and the need to spend on security.
Vulnerable small island nations say the cash they need to repair damage and to guard against future climate-related crises is again arriving too slowly and their own budgets have shrunk.

"Like many small island developing states, we remain in a perpetual climate disaster recovery mode," Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale told the conference. "We cannot build resilience while our fiscal space erodes."
Even when money is available, technical hurdles set by lenders can stretch the administrative capacity of small states.
For many developed nations, facing international and domestic unrest as citizens protest against the rising cost of living, their focus has narrowed.

Britain, which has sought to be a leader in addressing climate change, said in July savings made from switching some climate finance contributions from grants to loans would be used to help fund a cap on domestic bus fares.
Meanwhile, defence spending has climbed significantly.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimated in April that world military expenditure reached US$2.89 trillion in 2025, up 2.9 per cent in real terms from 2024.
Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine said military defence ultimately was the smaller concern.

"We are told there is no money, but as spending on war grows, the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death," she said in her speech to the conference in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya on Wednesday.
COP31 SEEKING IMPLEMENTATION, NOT NEW TARGETS

As they respond to the contemporary mood, host country Turkey and lead negotiator Australia have emphasised making previous pledges work, rather than securing a new headline target at the conference, which continues until the end of next week.

"COP31 must respond to the global moment and send a clear message to accelerate implementation," Australia's COP31 negotiating president Chris Bowen said. He also said finance must be "faster, simpler and fairer."

Analysis by previous COP host Brazil published earlier this week found that US$137 billion was mobilised in 2024, a slight increase on 2023, but that direct aid and future commitments to multilateral funds were lower.
Current trends suggested provision would fall US$840 billion short of the US$1.3 trillion goal, it said.
"Geopolitical tensions, constrained fiscal space in many developing countries and the high cost of capital where it is most needed are among the obstacles," the report said.
By way of solutions, it urged measures such as risk-sharing and clearer links between national plans and budgets.
Some smaller nations have taken novel steps to find cash and to spur richer nations to match it.
The Solomon Islands pledged US$400,000 from its own pocket on Thursday, saying it was determined to show leadership and calling on rich countries to do the same.
The Bahamas committed US$75 million to protect and restore its seagrass meadows, which store carbon, to try to persuade investors to fund verified carbon projects.
UNCLOGGING THE SYSTEM TO GET MONEY FLOWING
Both public and private funding provide climate finance grants, loans, aid and investment in measures ranging from renewable energy to flood defences.
Multilateral development banks are a conduit for finance that leverages capital provided by shareholder countries to increase lending power and they say they are delivering.
Their lending reached record levels in 2025, according to the European Investment Bank.
But, they could do more, according to Washington-based think tank the Center for Global Development and recipients of the finance have said the development banks should make access easier.

Addressing that, a group of multilateral funds told the COP31 talks they would rely more on one another's assessments in co-financed operations rather than having to go through multiple overlapping processes.
For private investors, the most obvious issue is the risk of investing in an instrument that does not guarantee returns.
Given how unforthcoming the world's richer governments have been, the private sector is ever more important.

"Our clients see opportunities in the energy transition, but they need reliable power, predictable costs and confidence in customer demand before they invest," HSBC Chief Sustainability Officer Julian Wentzel said.
"COP31 needs to help create that confidence."
* The writers are from Reuters

c93a199a2d31bc0a: MASJID TANAH: Ahli Parlimen Masjid Tanah Mas Ermieyati Samsudin mahu Bersatu memecatnya terus daripada parti itu, bukannya membiarkan status keahliannya terus tergantung tanpa sebarang perkembangan.
Beliau berkata sehingga kini tiada makluman baharu daripada kepimpinan Bersatu mengenai kedudukannya selepas digantung keahlian selama dua penggal pemilihan atau enam tahun, berkuat kuasa Mac lalu.
“Masih tergantung. Tak ada (perkembangan),” katanya kepada FMT ketika ditanya mengenai status keahliannya.
Bagaimanapun, Mas Ermieyati menegaskan tindakan disiplin itu tidak sedikit pun menjejaskan tugasnya sebagai wakil rakyat, malah beliau terus membantu kumpulan yang bersama dengannya.

“Tak, tak mengganggu. Tidak mengganggu langsung. Saya menggunakan kapasiti apa yang saya ada untuk membantu kawan-kawan dan juga pasukan yang lain bagi mencapai apa juga agenda yang telah pun diputuskan,” katanya.
Mengulas kedudukannya menjelang PRU akan datang, beliau menyerahkan keputusan sama ada mempertahankan kerusi Parlimen Masjid Tanah kepada pucuk pimpinan parti yang bakal diwakilinya.

Walaupun belum menyertai Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan), Mas Ermieyati menegaskan beliau kekal menyokong kepimpinan Ketua Pembangkang Hamzah Zainudin bersama kumpulan 13 Ahli Parlimen Bersatu yang menyokongnya.

Beliau turut merujuk kumpulan itu sebagai ‘Ahli Parlimen Reset’, selaras dengan gerakan diperkenalkan Hamzah, selain berpandangan dirinya tidak lagi terikat dengan Bersatu selepas pembubaran Parlimen.
Mas Ermieyati digantung keahlian Bersatu selama dua penggal pemilihan berkuat kuasa 10 Mac lalu selepas didapati melanggar Fasal 9.1.4 perlembagaan parti serta Kod Etika dan Tatakelakuan Ahli.
Tindakan itu menyusuli sokongan terbukanya terhadap Hamzah, yang dipecat daripada Bersatu pada 13 Feb lalu susulan kemelut kepimpinan parti.
Beliau adalah antara 13 Ahli Parlimen Bersatu yang menyokong Hamzah dan turut menghadiri perhimpunan menyokong bekas timbalan presiden parti itu pada 14 Feb, sehari selepas pemecatannya.
Hamzah sebelum ini melancarkan gerakan Reset sebagai usaha pembetulan, penambahbaikan dan pengukuhan kekuatan negara secara kolektif, sebelum menerajui Wawasan yang dilancarkan pada Jun lalu.
86701288745b438a: SHAH ALAM: Selangor has identified Kampung Melayu Subang, Kampung Kubu Gajah and Puncak Alam as priority areas for flood mitigation works.
Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari said the three areas experienced more serious flooding, particularly during the early stages of the Northeast Monsoon and monsoon transition periods.
The state has allocated RM36.45 million for 47 flood mitigation projects under its 2027 Budget.
He said the state government would review the locations earmarked for the projects based on current needs and ensure efforts to reduce flood risks continued.
"We will review them because this is an ongoing effort, and the three main areas are Kampung Melayu Subang, Kampung Kubu Gajah and Puncak Alam.
"These are three areas that experience serious flooding during the early stages of the monsoon or during the monsoon transition," he told reporters after officiating an education carnival.
Also present were Education Ministry Daily School Management Division director Mohd Hanafi Samad and Selangor Education Department director Datin Wan Nor Ashikin Abu Kassim.
Amirudin said Kuala Selangor also faced flooding, but problems in some areas, such as Parit Mahang, involved stagnant flooding and required specific attention as a longer-term issue.
He said the state government would seek to implement the projects as soon as possible and assess the effectiveness of flood mitigation measures in areas that had frequently been affected.
He said conditions had improved in several areas, including Dengkil and Kuala Langat, following mitigation efforts.
"These efforts will focus on 56 identified flood hotspots.
"Between 2016 and 2017, we had nearly 200 flood hotspots, but the number has since declined through the measures implemented, with several areas successfully addressed," he said.
b0660cbb84b52540: LONDON: The Daily Mail will boycott the final three races of the Formula One season after the FIA revoked veteran journalist Jonathan McEvoy's media credentials over an opinion column criticising Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc.

The British newspaper announced on Friday that it would not report on races or news conferences for the remainder of 2026 in protest of the FIA's decision to bar McEvoy from covering the Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix.
McEvoy, who has covered F1 for more than two decades, learned on Thursday that his accreditation had been withdrawn after a Nov 4 opinion column in which he called Leclerc a "sneaky little b......"

The criticism stemmed from an opening-lap incident at the Mexico City Grand Prix involving Leclerc and Ferrari teammate Lewis Hamilton. Both drivers went off the track while battling for the lead at Turn 4, with Leclerc cutting across the grass to emerge ahead and Max Verstappen passing Hamilton for second.
Leclerc subsequently received a five-second penalty for gaining an advantage off the track.

The FIA defended its decision, saying McEvoy's column "fell short of the standards of professionalism expected" from accredited journalists. The governing body said its accreditation guidelines allow it to revoke credentials without notice and stressed that the decision did not prevent the Daily Mail from sending another reporter.
Daily Mail head of sport Chris Dean called the punishment "an unprecedented and outrageous attack on the freedom of the Press" and demanded McEvoy's reinstatement.
In a subsequent column, McEvoy suggested that Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur had prompted the FIA's decision, although a Ferrari source told The Athletic that Vasseur had not lodged a complaint.
The Society of Editors also condemned the decision Friday, arguing that withdrawing accreditation over published criticism threatened independent sports journalism.
McEvoy said he was told his accreditation would be reinstated next season, although the FIA had not publicly confirmed that. - Reuters

d5fe56564f0e656a: NOVEMBER 15 — On November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver its judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar, a case concerning Myanmar’s alleged violations of the Genocide Convention. For our Rohingya community, this is more than a moment in international law. It follows decades of persecution and nearly ten years of waiting for the world to acknowledge what we have known: that we have endured a campaign of destruction because of who we are.
Yet, the conversation is being pulled away from the people whose lives are at stake.

In September, a Wall Street Journal opinion piece by Orde F. Kittrie and Andres B. Munoz-Mosquera warned that the ICJ could lower the legal threshold for establishing genocide in the Rohingya case. The authors connected this possibility to South Africa’s pending genocide case against Israel and potential claims against the United States, Nato members even suggesting sanctions against ICJ judges.

In October, US Ambassador Mike Waltz amplified this argument, warning against lowering the genocide threshold in ways that could affect American and allied soldiers. His remarks alongside Washington’s sanctions against the International Criminal Court, raised concerns about political pressure on international justice

Professor Michael Becker, former ICJ legal officer, explains that the Court’s treatment of genocidal intent could have repercussions for South Africa’s case against Israel particularly on how genocidal intent is inferred from patterns of conduct when states invoke military or counterterrorism operations.

That is a legitimate legal discussion. But the possibility that a judgment concerning the Rohingya could have consequences for another state is not a reason to politically contain the Rohingya case or prejudge the Court’s work.

As Professor John Packer reminds us, there is no adjustable genocide threshold to be lowered according to whose interests are affected. The law to be applied is the Genocide Convention. The question is whether the evidence satisfies its requirements.
International criminal lawyer Shyamala Alagendra shares my concern about the Rohingya proceedings being drawn into debates about other conflicts.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
In this file picture taken May 14, 2015 Rohingya migrants stand and sit on a boat drifting in Thai waters off the southern island of Koh Lipe in the Andaman sea. — AFP pic

She observed that the Court’s interpretation of the Genocide Convention will be relevant to other proceedings, but relevance is not equivalence. Each case must be determined on its own facts and evidence. The Court must neither shape its reasoning to assist another case nor hesitate to apply the law because of the consequences its judgment may have elsewhere.

Shyamala also distinguished legitimate criticism of the Court from attempts to influence its judgment: “judicial independence is not a privilege of judges, but a safeguard for those seeking justice and all whose rights and responsibilities are before the Court. It demands impartiality, fidelity to the law and the courage to decide without fear or favour.”
And yet, in all this discussion, I find myself asking a much more fundamental question: where are the Rohingya?

Where are the women and girls who survived the 2017 genocidal campaign? Where are the families who watched their homes disappear, their relatives killed and their communities emptied? Where are the children who have spent nearly a decade growing up in refugee camps, without citizenship, security or a meaningful prospect of returning home?

Multiple human rights reports have documented sexual violence against Rohingya women and girls during the 2017 military operations, alongside killings, village destruction and forced displacement. Those women did not leave their trauma behind when they crossed the Naf River into Bangladesh.

They carried it into the refugee camps, through fractured families, pregnancies and motherhood, and years of uncertainty. They have had to rebuild their lives without adequate access to healthcare, psychosocial support, justice or any assurance that they will not be forced to flee again.

The world has become remarkably comfortable discussing the Rohingya as a legal question, a humanitarian burden, a regional security concern or a diplomatic inconvenience. Drawing on her work with survivors of sexual and gender-based violence and crimes against children, Shyamala stressed that survivors must matter beyond their testimony and that the long-term consequences of these crimes can shape individual lives and reverberate across generations, affecting Rohingya everywhere, whether or not their suffering has entered the legal record.

And this is where I struggle with the direction of the current debate. If the concern is whether a finding against Myanmar might create legal exposure for another state, we have already lost sight of why this case exists.
For the Rohingya, this case is not a stepping stone. It is our case. It represents years of community organising, survivor testimony, documentation, advocacy and the determination.
We did not spend decades fighting erasure so that our suffering could become a footnote in somebody else’s legal argument.

Our conversation also turned to what happens after the judgment. Shyamala cautioned against confusing a legal milestone with justice delivered. The Genocide Convention imposes obligations beyond the courtroom in The Hague and states must consider what those obligations require in practice. Shyamala emphasised that even if the Court does not find Myanmar responsible for genocide, the atrocities suffered by the Rohingya remain, as does the possibility of responsibility for other international crimes. Nor should it provide a pretext for countries hosting Rohingya to diminish their protection. “Refugees do not have to establish that they are victims of genocide to deserve safety and dignity,” she observed.

A finding that Myanmar violated the Convention would be a historic step towards accountability. But it would not, by itself, return us home, restore our citizenship, recognise our ethnic identity or dismantle the systems that made genocide possible.

Rohingya-led universal jurisdiction initiatives, including my case as a lead complainant with Themis Indonesia, alongside the work of the Myanmar Accountability Project, demonstrate that our community is not waiting passively for one institution to determine its future.

Whatever the Court decides on November 19, our pursuit of justice will continue. But for now, let the Rohingya have this moment without being made collateral to somebody else’s geopolitical anxieties. When the judgement has been delivered and the legal arguments have moved elsewhere, we will still be here, living with its consequences and continuing our struggle for a place to call home.

c2500adde0f258db: LOS ANGELES, Nov 15 — The rhapsodic hip-hop transformers Wu-Tang Clan and punk rocker Billy Idol were among the music luminaries inducted Saturday into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame at a star-studded concert gala.

The versatile Phil Collins, post-punk and electronic dance music renegades Joy Division/New Order and the velvet-voiced late Luther Vandross also joined the rock pantheon at the ceremony held in Los Angeles’s Peacock Theater.
But several of the 2026 class of artists — Oasis, Sade and Iron Maiden — skipped the night celebrating their honor, one of the music industry’s most prestigious.
But the show went on.

Staten Island’s own Wu-Tang Clan — the ragtag group of New Yorkers who paired raw production with streetwise rhymes and martial arts influences — brought the ruckus, performing their own hits including C.R.E.A.M and Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nuthing ta F’ Wit.
“We went from being banned on the radio to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame,” said member Method Man onstage to resounding cheers.
To the haters, he said “you can kiss my inducted ass.”
It proved a banner night for women in hip-hop, with honorees including Queen Latifah as well as MC Lyte, who is widely recognised as the “First Lady of Hip Hop.”
The storied performers tore up the stage with a medley of their hits, before Megan Thee Stallion and Remy Ma joined them to underscore the legacy of women in rap.
Travis Barker, the drummer from Blink-182, inducted Collins, drawing tears from the British artist who attended the ceremony alongside his children including Lily of Emily in Paris fame.
Collins — whose entry into the hall is his second, the first was as part of the band Genesis — walked to the stage with two canes, taking the mic and saying “I’m really not as bad as it looks.”
“You haven’t heard the last of me, I can promise you that.”
Cynthia Erivo belted out Collins’s smash In The Air Tonight, with Barker playing the instantly recognizable drum fill.
“My life has just been one thing after the other, one dream after the other,” Collins said to journalists backstage.
Oasis a ‘dose of Viagra for the ego’
Punk rocker Billy Idol performed on behalf of himself after an induction from Gwen Stefani, delivering an electrifying version of his hit Rebel Yell.
Stefani later joined him onstage for a duet of Eyes Without a Face.
Idol took to the podium with Steve Stevens, his longtime guitarist who was also inducted.
“Punk was and remains a tremendously positive thing. Freedom to be yourself, freedom to be proud of our differences,” Idol said. “We are beautiful because we are true to ourselves.”
“And now I’m going to party with the Wu-Tang Clan!” the rocker shouted in closing.
In inducting no-shows Oasis, actor Bob Odenkirk called their music “a dose of Viagra for the ego.”
“Is anyone surprised they didn’t show up?” Odenkirk said to laughter. “They didn’t want to be here.”
“It would’ve been out of character if they had.”

Trent Reznor introduced the two British rock bands Joy Division and New Order, who got a rare joint induction. New Order formed from the ashes of Joy Division after the original group’s lead singer, Ian Curtis, died in 1980.
Bassist Peter Hook accepted the award on the group’s behalf.
‘Can’t kill rock’

Iron Maiden, who skipped as they’re touring in Australia, were honored by a supergroup of performers including St. Vincent, along with members of Rage Against the Machine and Metallica, and none other than Jack Black.
Oprah Winfrey introduced the legacy of the late Vandross, while Usher, another of music’s great crooners, delivered a rendition of Never Too Much.
Legendary television host Ed Sullivan, whose shows brought scores of musical acts to the masses, received the prestigious Ahmet Ertegun Award, which goes to a non-performing industry notable.
Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti and Gram Parsons were also among those honored, as was Rick Rubin, for whom Neil Young delivered a wide-ranging induction speech befitting the producer’s sweeping career.
The Red Hot Chili Peppers — dressed as Rubin lookalikes with sunglasses and long flowing white hair, as well as his signature wizard-esque beard — performed for the industry legend.
And Rubin delivered the night’s shortest speech.
“You can’t kill rock and roll,” he said. “Thank you.” — AFP
0bd59c113f40cddd: KUALA LUMPUR: The government should consider introducing mandatory Green Data Centre Certification to ensure that operators comply with measurable environmental performance standards, said Alliance for a Safe Community chairman Tan Sri Lee Lam Thye.

He said the rapid expansion of data centres in Malaysia, driven by growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and digital technology, must not come at the expense of environmental sustainability.
"Malaysia must strike the right balance between technological advancement, economic growth and environmental protection," he said in a statement today.

Lee called for stringent environmental requirements for major data centre developments, including assessments of their cumulative impact on electricity and water resources, as well as the surrounding environment.
He also proposed mandatory sustainability standards covering energy efficiency, water consumption and carbon emissions, supported by regular independent audits.
He said data centre operators should progressively increase their use of renewable energy and adopt more energy-efficient cooling technologies to reduce pressure on the national electricity grid.

On water security, he expressed concern that the substantial volume of water required for cooling operations could affect local communities, particularly in areas already facing water supply challenges.
He urged operators to prioritise recycled and reclaimed water, rainwater harvesting and water-efficient cooling technologies rather than relying excessively on treated drinking water.
"The construction of large data centre facilities may involve extensive land clearing, potentially affecting green spaces, biodiversity, natural habitats and local drainage systems," he said.
In addition, he called for greater accountability in managing electronic waste generated through the replacement of servers, batteries and other equipment.
To improve transparency, Lee said data centre operators should be required to disclose their electricity and water consumption, carbon emissions and overall environmental performance.
He said the government should review investment incentives and approval conditions to ensure that companies receiving government incentives demonstrate genuine commitments to sustainable development.

He said data centre development must be planned according to the availability of electricity, water and supporting infrastructure to avoid placing additional burdens on public utilities and local communities.
"Digital transformation must not become an environmental burden. Economic progress must not compromise our water security, energy sustainability and quality of life," he said.

7748b53d45b4eebd: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all.
The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children.

The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories."

Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids.

Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it.

LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013. It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge.

The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011. The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory.

The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948.

EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I. ®
cdcf6741ad88380d: MANAMA: Blasts rang out over Bahrain early on Sunday as Iran's Guards said they attacked a US military base in the Gulf nation, which has been heavily targeted during the Middle East war.
Sirens sounded and authorities posted several alerts on social media urging residents to seek shelter, their first warnings since September.
After a lull in attacks, Bahrain, which hosts a major US naval base, has been targeted twice in three days. The energy-rich Gulf has borne the brunt of Iranian strikes during the war.
Bahrain's military said it intercepted several Iranian attacks, "preventing them from reaching their intended targets". The foreign ministry said air defence systems shot down Iranian drones.
Explosions could be heard around 4.00am (0100 GMT), an AFP journalist said, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6.30am.
The interior ministry, posting on X, called on "residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels".
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their forces carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a base, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster.

"The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the Guards said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response," it added.

During more than eight months of war, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz oil trade route and struck infrastructure, including airports, seaports, energy facilities, and US assets across the region.
Bahrain is among the Gulf countries that have weathered thousands of Iranian drone and missile strikes since the war began on Feb 28.

The tiny island nation "rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences", the foreign ministry statement said.
On Friday, the Revolutionary Guards said their forces targeted a US early warning radar system in Bahrain – the first strike against a Gulf country since early September.
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said it shot down two Iranian drones targeting the Gulf island, reporting no casualties or damage in the attack.
CENTCOM, which oversees American military operations in the region, said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil since the summer via Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump, whose steep reverse in midterm elections was partly blamed on the Iran war, plans to discuss the conflict at a trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts this week, an official said Friday.
Months of diplomacy have failed to resolve the war, which began with surprise US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

76eaaf5e86a317f5: SEREMBAN, Nov 15 — Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) must use its defeats in several state elections as a springboard to strengthen the party and prepare its machinery for the 16th General Election (GE16), its vice-president Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said.
